prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the Z2 quantum spin Hall state and its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells, which established symmetry-protected topological insulators

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B006 to B013 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a single part. I ranked B013 eighth because it is outside my field, and the first round gave me what I needed to judge it on my own criterion, which is experimental closure. The prediction was specific and could have failed: spin-orbit coupling and time-reversal symmetry give a Z2 invariant with protected edge channels. The HgTe experiment then measured the signature quantitatively, a conductance near 2e^2/h that survives in a short, narrow device and is lost in a wide one, with gate-voltage dependence that excludes trivial explanations. Johansson makes this point well in his reply to me. Transport, ARPES and scanning-probe work in many materials and laboratories have confirmed it for almost two decades, so maturity is not in question. I also accept that the six explicit supporters are largely independent readers of the same record, and that the chair cautions about convergence following from reading each other's openings. My move rests on the scientific closure and on the attribution being workable, not on the count. The trio fits the three-person limit and follows who did what first.
statement.case_against: The allocation is the weak point and I do not want to hide it. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal told Molenkamp where to look and sits outside the credited names, with Zhang deceased, and Hasan's 3D ARPES work is a serious experimental discovery that a 2D-focused trio leaves out. Any citation must be careful not to claim more than the three people did. The 2016 prize on topological phases and phase transitions is a real thematic neighbour, and I cannot say on my own authority that the overlap is harmless. Device payoff is thin so far, which matters to me more than to most colleagues, though I accept it is not the statutory test. Finally, B006 remains in my view an equally clean two-name case, and I am giving it up as my first choice because the committee sees broader scientific reach in B013, not because I think the clocks are weak.

responses.point: Olsson asked what discovery claim I would put in a B006 citation beyond record accuracy, and said device maturity is the wrong yardstick for this prize. She also notes that Hasan's photoemission work is an original experiment and that any trio excludes someone with a serious claim.
responses.response: The question is fair and I cannot answer it well enough. The most I can say for B006 is that it combined many-atom statistics with recoil-free trapping and opened a regime of precision comparison, and that reads as a capability and not a new phenomenon. For a prize I accept that the quantum spin Hall effect, a state of matter nobody had seen, is the stronger discovery claim, and that is part of why I moved. On Hasan I agree the cost is real. I still do not see how to include him within three names without removing Kane or Mele, and I think the citation should be honest by restricting itself to the quantum spin Hall line and not suggest the 3D branch is covered.

responses.point: Eriksson, as reported in the chair summary and in my round-1 reading of his file, prefers Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan and leaves Mele out, arguing that first-principles band theory with ARPES and transport agree quantitatively and that recognition is overdue.
responses.response: I accept his criterion of theory-experiment closure and it is a large part of why I now favour B013. I still hold that Mele should not be dropped. Kane and Mele published the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall proposal together, and removing one of them in order to fit Hasan makes the theory half of the story harder to defend than the Hasan omission is. If the committee overrides me and insists on Hasan, the fairer swap would be a debate about the relative priority of the 3D discovery against the 2D, not a quiet removal of one theorist, and I would want that argued explicitly with the citation rewritten to cover topological insulators as a class. For now I prefer the narrower and more accurate trio and the narrower citation.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that symmetry-protected band topology in real materials is distinct from the 2016 topological phase-transition prize, but that the citation must say so clearly, and he worries that a decisive step (Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang) goes unrecognised.
responses.response: I agree with the distinction and would answer the chair's question with one sentence: the 2016 prize recognised topological phase transitions and Hall-type phases in model systems, whereas this one recognises a prediction of a time-reversal-protected topological state from spin-orbit coupling in a band insulator and its quantitative observation in a real material. That is why my citation names the Z2 quantum spin Hall state and the HgTe observation explicitly. I would not go as far as Danielsson's and Olsson's wording about establishing a new class of matter, since that edges into the 3D branch which the trio does not cover, and I have kept only the narrower phrasing about symmetry-protected topological insulators following from these two steps. On the missing BHZ credit, no citation fixes it, and the committee's background material should state it openly.

responses.point: Mehlig answers my round-1 point that device payoff is scarce by saying the statutes ask for a discovery or invention of importance, that applications are not required, and that the 2016 citation did not cover symmetry-protected band topology with spin-orbit coupling.
responses.response: I accept this. My preference for measurement-led impact is a personal weighting and not the test, and the quantum Hall effect was physics before it was metrology. His point that the idea has spread into photonics, cold atoms and mechanical systems also answers my question about whether it has opened a field. I would keep the evidence base visible in the committee's documentation, with the HgTe width and gate dependence and the later ARPES confirmations, so that the claim of reproducibility rests on measurements and not on the number of members who agree.

responses.point: Lindroth reads B006 as a performance record on a field recognised in 2005 and 2012, and prefers B002, while naming B013 as her first alternative and acknowledging that she may overweight her own field.
responses.response: I partly agree with her reading of B006, and I accept it as one reason the discovery claim is weaker than for B013. On B002, I think her own list of problems (five credited names for three seats, Jaksch uncredited, the platform-versus-discovery question) is the reason it does not beat B013 for me either. Since we each name B013 as the first alternative and neither of us finds a flaw in its physics, I do not think a second part is needed. A second part would also require splitting the three-person limit, which no combination of her B002 trio or my Katori and Ye can do alongside Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. I would keep B006 and B022 on the table for a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a narrow 2D quantum spin Hall citation that leaves out Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, or whether it prefers a broader citation on topological insulators that the three named people cannot fully support.
Whether the one-sentence distinction from the 2016 prize will satisfy the colleagues who raised the overlap, since I rely on them for the condensed-matter specifics.
My assessment of B013 comes from reading colleagues' accounts of the HgTe and ARPES evidence and not from my own work, so I may be underweighting an experimental caveat I would see in my own field.
Priority between Katori's lattice-clock proposal and parallel work around 2003 to 2005, which I could not verify and which now matters only for the alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict applies to B013: I have no collaboration, mentorship or institutional link with Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or Hasan. My earlier disclosure stands for the other candidates: no tie to B006 candidates, though my mentor Sune Svanberg and my PhD-period host John Hall are in the precision-spectroscopy tradition, and an institutional overlap with Goran Johansson through the Chalmers-led WACQT, relevant to B009 only. My rare-earth quantum-memory work and Deep Light Vision interests are not connected to any shortlisted candidate. I have not asked for recusal on any item.
